meta.title: Do I belong in tech anymore?
meta.author: Shorden

comments.author: technomancy
comments.text: I left my job a month ago for similar reasons; I felt like my job was to provide adult supervision to the people on my team who had given up thinking for themselves. It was honestly terrifying to watch their ability decay over the course of a year, in some cases going from a skilled, trusted professional to someone regularly making junior level mistakes several times a week. It was sad to see what I had spent years building fall apart so quickly, but I had to get out. Luckily I found another gig where I wasn't required to use any LLM stuff, hope others can do the same.

comments.author: Vaelatern
comments.text: "BI." Fascinating tool to me that I wish to use someday in a context where it may make sense to pay money to the team that runs it.

comments.author: Vaelatern
comments.text:
This is doubly astonishing to me since LLMs have proven terrible to me at writing Clojure. I think there is a disjoint relationship between things that are Fun To Write (Clojure, lisps, etc.) and things that LLMs are good at (boilerplate lovers like Java, and I hate to say it because I love it but it's true, Go).

Your previous job used a language LLMs are not good at writing, mostly because that language focuses so much on developers having a good time it never asked if LLMs would too.

comments.author: henrycatalinismith
comments.text:
Ironically, what I’ve gained from AI is a deeper appreciation for human communication, in all its messy imperfection. The point of a code review is not simply for good code to make it into a codebase, but to build institutional knowledge as people debate and iterate and compromise, slow as it may be. Friction is good.


Felt this.

Time was you might give the same piece of code review feedback to the same person five to ten times and then the knowledge would probably stick for them. We were helping each other to grow at the same time as we produced code.

Agent adoption beyond a certain threshold takes that away. Your code review feedback is just another prompt for the agent. The person who's nominally running the agent doesn't have time to read and internalise any of the actual ideas expressed, because the whole point of why they're even using the agent is to save exactly the time they would have spent doing that for running more agents.

I get that agents open some doors but the whole philosophy of work that's inherent to really extreme adoption does seem to structurally relegate human communication outside the critical path of the work. My current job is nowhere near as extreme as the workplace described in this post and I hope it never is. It sounds very very lonely.

comments.author: ironick
comments.text:
We know at work who are the big users of AI. I have noticed a big trend in our code reviews.

The AI power users consistently require the most detailed reviews, with obvious UI breaks on their branches that you’d never miss if you were looking at the result of your change.

But more to the point, I will consistently give, say a comment of feedback on a particular way of approaching something and offer a suggestion to fix it, mentioning that “this is a better way to do this”/“more consistent with the codebase” etc etc

over and over, they will fix only the instance of that issue that the comment was pegged to, leaving the rest of the PR untouched when the same issue was present multiple times, even when I mention those other instances in the original comment

And then more PRs come through with the same issues, and I keep on having to essentially go line by line and tell them each instance to fix

All in all, I just know that these people are not reading the code they submit, and are not able to implement feedback or take it on board because they’re not concerned with the quality of the code in the first place

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text:
over and over, they will fix only the instance of that issue that the comment was pegged to, leaving the rest of the PR untouched when the same issue was present multiple times, even when I mention those other instances in the original comment


The weird thing is LLMs are actually quite good at pattern amplification: you can fix one case yourself and ask the LLM to fix everything else in the PR/diff — it'll be more complete about it than a human could be. Your colleagues are definitely not doing that, which is unfortunate. (Speaking as someone who used LLMs extensively for a while but has become a bit more circumspect lately.)

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: Quite true, the current crop of LLMs is fantastic at doing refactors and cleanups. If you understand the code well enough to tell them what you want refactored or cleaned up.

comments.author: mwcampbell
comments.text: I'm curious about why you've become more circumspect in your use of LLMs. Not wanting to argue or even gain ammunition for a particular argument, just curious. Thanks.

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text:
Over a few months I've had one pretty rough bug slip through, and another instance where I fixed a (pre-existing) bug as part of some feature work but didn't realize the severity/urgency of the bug until a few months later. Thankfully, no production code paths exercised either bug, but neither would have been likely to happen were I not using them. Both those incidents were below the standard I hold myself to.

On the other hand, LLMs have also caught a number of defects in my hand-written code (things like unsafe code invariants breaking under panics), so they clearly have real utility.

comments.author: Loup-Vaillant
comments.text:
Sounds like people who should be… perhaps not fired right away, but at the very least put on a Performance Improvement Plan as soon as possible. Regardless of whether they’re using AIs or not, what you’re reporting is:


Consistently submitting obvious mistakes they should have checked themselves.

Consistently failing to apply feedback consistently.

Consistently wasting your time, in part by not changing their behaviour after your code reviews.


I’d guess they also consistently submit crap code. Anyway, regardless of the tools they use: LLM, sub-contractor from the Global South, or just their own brain, I’d guess they’re more trouble than they’re worth — at least for now.

comments.author: danking
comments.text:
over and over, they will fix only the instance of that issue that the comment was pegged to, leaving the rest of the PR untouched when the same issue was present multiple times


I have had the same experience.

I wonder if my nits and gripes even matter. The AI-inclined amongst us produce a lot of code. That code does something. Do its little warts, failures, deceptions, etc. matter? The world is transitioning to a low-trust relationship with many products.

LLMs maybe give you an answer to the question you intended to ask. Now products maybe do what you intended to request.

I kinda think that the vast majority of software that people use never needed to met the standards I set for the software that I use.

comments.author: julik
comments.text:
Time was you might give the same piece of code review feedback to the same person five to ten times and then the knowledge would probably stick for them. We were helping each other to grow at the same time as we produced code.


Which is also a very cruel way to teach - if there is anything from "back in the day" that I won't be missing - it is this. We were doing this, but we were also misled as to what's more important - teaching or delivering working software. I am all for mentoring and teaching, but I would not do it this way. People who did often did so out of pettiness (case in point: I know of a changeset consisting of a dev script that could not get landed for 3 months, and not for lack of trying).

comments.author: txxnano
comments.text:
I'll say it's all in the first paragraph


Does any of this work actually matter?

Aside of this, I'll say I'm a bit tired of reading posts like this and I'm under the impression that we, programmers, need to be a bit more detached from the current day to day job and take it as other professionals: as a job

Furthermore, and this completely personal opinion, I believe this post it's simply too negative with statements like


Ethically: Generative AI tools, powered by data centers which consume vast amounts of water and pollute our environment, are built on the collective theft of the works of millions of artists, developers, authors, and other creatives, supercharge the spread of disinformation and fascism, have repeatedly provoked psychosis and suicide, and concentrate wealth in fewer hands while providing cover for widespread layoffs.


Yes but no, many of these issues are and were caused by political movements and think tanks outside technology, and we are blaming just all to AI tools or Palantir; it's just an escape goat. AI didn't vote (yet). I'll recommend to watch Trauma Zone by Adam Curtis

Eventually and as Christopher Alexander used to say, we will connect as humans, making computers do computer stuff

comments.author: elephantium
comments.text:
With productivity gains over the past century, we could have been at 1-2 day work weeks if the gains had been equally distributed.

I do think that falls apart for other reasons.  For a lot of work, continuity matters.  For myself, I have to work harder on Mondays to get back in the frame of mind for whatever I was working on last week.

There's also the standard of living.  If we had steadily dropped working hours to match productivity, the standard of living would be a lot closer to conditions in the 1950s.  That's kind of a mixed bag in some ways (housing, education, health care), but a huge loss in others (energy efficient houses, automobile safety, better passenger jets, cell phones at all, etc).

comments.author: hjvt
comments.text: I don't get the connection you're making between work hours per week and cell phones existing. Automobile safety largely improved due to regulations, not due to free market R&D. Passenger jets, I'd imagine, could actually evolve faster with 3 day weekends being enough to jump on a flight somewhere, spend most of two days there and comeback.

comments.author: elephantium
comments.text:
Oh, the connection is simply that if you're working less, the world overall gets less.  New inventions and technical improvements take time and productivity to come to fruition.  If we were all working less, I'm assuming that new innovations would take longer to get to market.  For automobile  safety, think about airbags.  You can't have regulations mandating them before they exist.  For passenger jets, yeah, maybe in a shorter-work-week scenario, you'd have more market pressure to provide more flights.  OTOH, if the market is now working less, the market can't afford extra flights.

The more I think on this topic, the more I think that even distribution of the gains would just mean "we all buy more toys!" with just a few contrarian outliers.

comments.author: hjvt
comments.text:
Oh, I think the core of our disagreement is the definition of "work".

When I talk about "workweek" I mean wage labour, selling your time to feed yourself. If I had a 4 day work week, I'd have a hell of a lot more time for my hobbies. I have a cabinet full of electronics parts for guitar pedals that I've been too busy to "work" with. I have my "virtual eurorack synth" project that's been waiting in a barely usable state for me to "work" on it's UI/UX for close to two years now. At least I got my recipe for Hungarian-inspired split pea soup tuned to near perfection.

Leaving me alone, there's recently been a spree of a few prolific Rust-lang maintainers announcing stepping back due to no longer being sponsored to work on it. Just imagine how much more man-hours would opensource projects receive if only every one of us had an extra day free from labouring for some corporation of questionable ethics! Hell, even Google understands this (or at least used to) with their "20% side project time" policy.

I do not find your line of reasoning particularly compelling. To analogise, do you think A. G. Bell would have invented the telephone, if he had to work 50 hour weeks, commute included?

comments.author: Loup-Vaillant
comments.text:
Yes but no , many of these issues are and were caused by political movements and think tanks outside technology


Let’s unpack the paragraph you’re quoting.



Generative AI tools [are] powered by data centers which consume vast amounts of water and pollute our environment



Such resource consumption and pollution is kind of a requirement for AI to exist at all. You want more models, more users? You gotta have more data centres, consume more resources, and pollute quite a bit more. Speaking of which, infrasound seems to be a significant health issue for many people leaving near data centres.



Generative AI tools […], are built on the collective theft of the works of millions of artists, developers, authors, and other creatives



Again, this data collection is necessary to get good models. The only alternative would be to pay all the authors, which would likely cost more in paperwork than in copyright fees themselves. In fact, I suspect doing this correctly and ethically is likely to instantly invalidate the entire business model.

To nuance that a bit I do have issue with the term "theft" here: copyright is state granted monopoly, not actual property. Still, to the extent we accept copyright law is a good thing, there’s something wrong with the data collection necessary to teach an AI. Even if you reduced the scope of copyright to commercial exploitation and 5 years after publication, scrapping a recent news article so ChatGPT can be better at predicting the next word is a copyright violation. It’s not obvious if you frame it as "learning" and "generating" or "predicting", but I believe it’s more accurate to see models as a form of lossy compression.



Generative AI tools […], have repeatedly provoked psychosis and suicide



Significant effort needs to be spent on safety to avoid things like that, and that effort diverts resources the company could instead devote to promotion or making the model even more powerful. In fact, this is not specific to AI at all, this is just the usual tension between profitability (or competitiveness), and externalised risks so typical of our economy. Not sure we can really fix that one, short of addressing Capitalism itself. A highly political issue for sure, but one born out of the status quo, not any particular political movement.



Generative AI tools […] supercharge the spread of disinformation and fascism,



Disinformation in general, well… they do so in two ways: hallucinations, and helping people spread believable lies. The first problem is mostly technical. The second problem is more about giving people powerful tools. As for fascism… given than authoritarians are more likely to value hierarchies and in-group thinking instead of truth, I’m not surprised generative AI favours the far right more than it favours the far left here. Structurally I mean, not because any interest or political movement leaned in particularly heavily.

And do not forget the other side of the equation: recommendation algorithms and filters. There’s a reason it’s hard to widely publish, say, porn of people way too young to be legal: the biggest platforms have filters in place so they do not recommend those things, or even host them at all. The same could be said for political discourse. See what happened to the Overton window on Twitter after Musk took over. I believe this side is much more responsible for misinformation and fascism than generative AI is.

I do have to concede however that Grok is a case of a very rich, very political, not-that-technical dude causing the harm. Clearly, Grok wouldn’t so easily spout Nazi nonsense without someone like Musk in charge. Still, Grok wouldn’t be so harmful if Twitter wasn’t such an enabler.



Generative AI tools […] concentrate wealth in fewer hands while providing cover for widespread layoffs.



Again, a very general point about infrastructure being captured by, and profiting, rich capitalists instead of everyone else. Again, status quo, not any particular movement. And the solution is the same: public investments, tax the rich, regulate…

One way to look at this is to say that most of these issues were present since Capitalism is a thing, and AI, just like looms, is just one of many technologies that was captured by the system to concentrate wealth, at the expense of pretty much everything else. Then yes, this is all about political movements and think tanks outside of tech, and solving the root of the problems gets us way out of scope for this forum.

On the other hand, generative AI does uniquely amplify those problems, so avoid using it, and telling everyone we should stop using it, may very well be the only ethical way forward, given the society we’re currently living in. Wait, no, there’s also blowing up those data centres, but I’d rather not encourage crimes in any legislation where it is illegal to do so.

comments.author: Ameo
comments.text:
Your co-workers were like this before AI was a thing.  Leadership had the same narrow and close-minded view of you and your job before AI too.  You were judged in very similar ways then as you are now.  The value of what you do hasn't changed at all, and as other commenters have said it probably never mattered that much and never will.

AI just amplifies what was there already.  The fact that the golden age of Silicon Valley has gone and software devs aren't a rare in-demand hero contributes to this as well.

As far as the political stuff you talk about, I largely think that follows with the fact that the balance of power has shifted from employee to employer in tech in a lot of places.  This year, for the first time in my career, I felt like I was in direct competition with my coworkers for my job rather than working with them as a team.

AI companies care about profits and growth more than things like the greater good, the environment, or whatever.  Just like all the other companies in the world.  Politicians and other people in positions of power use AI to entrench and reinforce their power, just like all other technology.

And yeah, AI kind of sucks as a person who puts value in their ability to write code.  I've not been in flow state since 2025 and it used to be something I experienced more days than not.


idk what position I'm even taking here.  I guess I'm just using this as an opportunity to vent or something.   Who cares.

comments.author: quasilyte
comments.text:
I like to write code.

Living in a world when you're treated like a weird guy for wanting to write-and-understand the code is not feeling rewarding. No. It feels demoralizing. For now, I'll consider getting back to making games - it's very crappy in terms of the money (barely enough to cover the cheaper country monthly rent), but at least I can choose to do the things my way :)

comments.author: jorgelbg
comments.text:
I find particularly interesting how AI has become the way of ditching a lot of established patterns in the name of solving a bottleneck that was never the problem to begin with. Some of these I've shared among my colleagues in random coffee chats, and we tend to agree:

Code reviews, theoretically not needed (nor practical with the volume of slop generated by the models). Code reviews were never about verifying each line per-se. From my PoV it was more about knowledge sharing among the team, sometimes learning of a different way and to understand why maybe something that it is working would not scale or would not be the best approach. Also avoiding the tunnel vision that we all get when expending a lot of time focusing on a single outcome.

Understanding code, yep this is apparently is not needed anymore and very much related to the previous item. Architecture of the code, putting the right abstractions in place, improving the tests.

Number of lines written as a proxy to productivity and/or value added to a project/code base.

If we squint a bit tho, it is not only sane technical practices going away, we are now back to "managers" (or CEOs) enforcing tools onto developers. We had an agreement that enforcing tooling into developers that is meant to be used by the developers was a bad idea, unless we are talking about agents, models, LLMs, which is apparently the golden path now. Forcing people to "prompt their way to success" instead of just writing code and using whatever means to make the most progress its going out the window.

comments.author: toastal
comments.text: Seems fine to me as I’ve been feeling the same. After going thru stages of grief, I’m less hyperfocused on trying to level up on tech skills. I’m playing games with friends, looking to dabble in art again, looking at starting a small local business. It’s been more freeing to stop trying to fight it when it seems the loudest ones no longer care about the philosophy or learning—it’s all just vibes man. If I do find some work, I would be more fulfilled to program something for me, my business, or my local community.

comments.author: james
comments.text:
When I started full-time design and dev work in the 2010s, tech was generally understood to be a progressive place.
Tech organizations have now given up on pushing back against
What happened to the principles that were professed a decade ago?


Anyone asking these kinds of questions or perceiving a change in trend in this time period is absolutely delusional. 99% of tech exists in the space of extreme exploitation through being involved in forwarding goals in finance, adtech or other exploitative extractive organisations (e.g. Amazon). Show me someone who's working in a tech job that thinks that it's 'progressive' in some way that is measurably and provably socially good and I'll show you someone either absolutely delusional, able to compartmentalise the work they do in their tech job so they don't have to deal with the actual social effects of the real use of the tech they build, or one of the very very few lucky people who gets to build systems with tech which have net positive social effect.

Tech is just part of the social and political system. If you live in a western country, tech is employed primarily in the service of the goals of your society, and at this point in history (and for at least the last 50 years), these goals have been primarily capitalist. If you didn't realise that until now, I'm glad you do now, but to consider this a change is so delusional I'm just continually shocked at the number of people working in tech who have so little social and political awareness that they're only now perceiving a change or like there is something wrong. This is not a change. Tech and capitalism have been intertwined and bedfellows for a long time. And to blame the change on just the current superficially most present and visible tech artefact is similarly just disappointing - this is nothing to do with whatever the current most visible output of tech is (and hasn't been since that most visible thing was a loom or a steam engine), it has to do with the systems we choose to live in which make those things able to be used for exploitation and to service capital and power.
